paper.title: LASER: LLM Agent with State-Space Exploration for Web Navigation
paper.central_claim: Modelling an interactive web task as state-space exploration, where the LLM agent moves among a small pre-defined set of states with state-specific instructions and permissible actions, enables flexible backtracking and always-valid actions; guided only by state-specific instructions without in-context examples, LASER significantly outperforms previous methods on WebShop and closes the gap with human performance on amazon.com. Scope as measured: WebShop shopping task (500 test instructions) and 100 amazon.com instructions, GPT-4-0613.

evidence.quote: Experimental results show that LASER significantly outperforms previous methods and closes the gap with human performance on the web navigation task.
evidence.support_explanation: Author headline claim.

evidence.quote: previous methods implicitly assume a forward-only execution mode for the model, where they only provide oracle trajectories as in-context examples to guide the model on how to reason in the environment.
evidence.support_explanation: Author-stated gap 1: forward-only execution, no recovery.

evidence.quote: Moreover, previous methods assume a global action space where the model is free to take any action at any step
evidence.support_explanation: Author-stated gap 2: global action space leads to invalid actions.

evidence.quote: we consider an agent to be in two different states only if the structure of the current environment observation is different.
evidence.support_explanation: State definition: a handful of hand-categorised observation layouts.

evidence.quote: Our LASER requires manual annotation of possible states in the environment and their corresponding descriptions.
evidence.support_explanation: Hand-authored structure; domain-specific by design.

evidence.quote: ReAct (ours rerun) 34.0 59.7 WebGUM Furuta et al. (2023) 45.0 67.5 LASER - backup 48.4 71.2 LASER 50.0 75.6
evidence.support_explanation: Main WebShop results (success rate, reward) on 500 test instructions.

evidence.quote: ASH Lo et al. (2023) 30.2 56.7 ReAct Yao et al. (2023) * 40.0 66.6
evidence.support_explanation: Prior ASH and original ReAct (simplified setting, PaLM) numbers copied from prior work.

evidence.quote: We used 500 test set instructions for evaluation and adopted reward and success rate as metrics following previous works
evidence.support_explanation: Evaluation set and metrics.

evidence.quote: We used GPT-4-0613 to power LASER and its function-calling ability to implement action selection step.
evidence.support_explanation: Backbone and implementation of action selection.

evidence.quote: Despite our best efforts, the agent still makes invalid actions in some cases and achieves worse results than the original paper.
evidence.support_explanation: The authors own ReAct rerun underperforms the originally published ReAct (34.0 vs 40.0): baseline fidelity caveat.
amazon.com transfer results vs human reference from the WebShop paper.

evidence.quote: We follow the same settings as Yao et al. (2022) and evaluated on 100 test set instructions and then manually evaluated results.
evidence.support_explanation: Amazon evaluation size and manual annotation.

evidence.quote: we follow Yao et al. (2022) and conducted human evaluation.
evidence.support_explanation: Item attribute/option/category matches annotated by the authors, no inter-annotator check described.

evidence.quote: LASER 52.0 77.6 LASER + One-shot 50.0 74.9 LASER - function call 50.0 76.2 LASER (text-davinci-003) 38.5 70.2
evidence.support_explanation: Ablations on 200 instructions.

evidence.quote: Due to the limited computing budget, we only ran our ablation studies on 200 instructions.
evidence.support_explanation: Ablation sample size.

evidence.quote: Since LASER already performs valid actions 100% time, we hypothesize that the agent understands the task well without in-context examples
evidence.support_explanation: Valid-action rate stated (no table; no baseline rate given).

evidence.quote: We manually annotated 30 error cases from the Dev set to understand the failure cases of LASER.
evidence.support_explanation: Failure audit on 30 dev errors: 9 item-good-enough, 12 retrieval failure, 9 missing details.

evidence.quote: We found 12 out of 30 cases fall into this category.
evidence.support_explanation: Retrieval failure share (search engine, not the agent).

evidence.quote: Therefore, all baselines we considered use some kind of human knowledge/prior to help the agent learn.
evidence.support_explanation: Authors frame LASER as injecting high-level human knowledge instead of trajectories.

evidence.quote: We believe that providing high-level generalizable instructions (as done in LASER) is a more efficient ways of learning than providing low-level task-specific trajectories (e.g. WebGUM).
evidence.support_explanation: Author belief, untested by an effort comparison.

evidence.quote: When the agent is forced to stop after the maximum number of steps, it selects one of the intermediate results as the final output, and we call this the backup strategy.
evidence.support_explanation: Backup strategy raises LASER from 48.4/71.2 to 50.0/75.6.

evidence.quote: We allow our agent to make 15 state transitions in maximum.
evidence.support_explanation: Step budget of LASER; baseline budgets are not stated.

evidence.quote: we forced the agent to stop when it decides to buy the item when experimenting on amazon.com
evidence.support_explanation: No purchase actually executed on the live site.

evidence.quote: In this work, we have only experimented with the task of finding the target item for the shopping domain.
evidence.support_explanation: Single-domain scope.

evidence.quote: Most similar to our work, Synapse Zheng et al. (2024b) also proposed to use state-conditional prompts to guide the LLM
evidence.support_explanation: Nearest neighbour per the authors; Synapse decomposes few-shot examples.

evidence.quote: For the WebShop task, we define a total of four states, and the full prompts for search, results, and item states can be found in Table 4 , Table 5 and Table 6 in the appendix.
evidence.support_explanation: Prompts are disclosed (Tables 4-8).

evidence.quote: Specifically, we define a set of permissible actions that the agent can choose from for each state, which ensures that the agent always performs valid actions.
evidence.support_explanation: Per-state action masking by function lists.

evidence.quote: Naturally, this allows the agent to easily recover from a wrong action: taking another action that would send it back to the previous state.
evidence.support_explanation: Backtracking mechanism claim.

evidence.quote: Each action is implemented as a function call following the guidelines from OpenAI
evidence.support_explanation: Action space implemented as OpenAI function calls.

evidence.quote: The agent accumulates all of the past observations, thoughts, and actions in its prompt, using a full trajectory of exploration as an in-context example.
evidence.support_explanation: ReAct baseline description (in-context full trajectory).

evidence.quote: However, the drop is less significant compared to the observation made for ReAct and ASH agent
evidence.support_explanation: Robustness to longer trajectories asserted from a figure not in the text.

evidence.quote: we think extra caution and testing are required before deploying LASER to real-world scenarios.
evidence.support_explanation: Authors flag risk and need for human verification.

evidence.quote: defining state machines ( Ma et al., 2023 )
evidence.support_explanation: A sibling paper in this batch lists LASER (Ma et al.) as the state-machine approach; supports the lineage reading only.

Our arithmetic from reported n: WebShop n=500 gives SE about 2.2 points per method; LASER 50.0 vs WebGUM 45.0 is about 1.6 combined SE; vs the authors ReAct rerun 34.0 it is about 5 SE. Ablation n=200 (SE about 3.5 points): differences of 1.6-2.0 points (one-shot 50.0, no function call 50.0 vs 52.0) are inside noise. Amazon n=100 (SE about 4.9 points): 62.0 vs human 65.0 is not distinguishable.

Searched main text, Tables 1-8, Limitations, Appendices A-E for: token/latency/dollar cost, number of LLM calls per episode, sampling temperature, repeated runs or seeds, an ablation that removes the state formulation or the per-state action restriction while keeping the same instructions, counts of backtracking events, an invalid-action rate for baselines, and the date of the amazon.com experiments. None reported. Figure values (trajectory-length plot) are images.

signatures.name: State-conditioned instruction and action space
signatures.object: Prompt/action interface of a prompted web agent (baseline: global action space plus in-context demonstration trajectory)
signatures.information: Text observation of WebShop page; hand-written state taxonomy (four states), per-state system prompt with a placeholder layout, goal and rules; per-state function list; history of thoughts and actions.
signatures.operation: Classify the environment into a state; present that state prompt and its permissible action functions; the model writes a rationale (thought) and then a function call chosen from those functions; each action leads deterministically to another or the same state (e.g. results -> item, item -> results by Prev, results -> search by Back_to_Search).
signatures.output: A single valid function call per step.
signatures.conditions: A small number of observation layouts can be enumerated by hand (e-commerce, travel booking); function-calling capable LLM.
signatures.selection_rule_data: None: LLM chooses among permissible actions.
signatures.persistence: None across episodes; prompts are fixed.
signatures.claimed_effect: 100% valid actions; flexible backtracking; WebShop SR 50.0 / reward 75.6.
signatures.failure_boundary: Manual annotation; single-domain; retrieval failures (12/30) and wrong-item errors (9/30 missing details) remain.

signatures.name: Backtracking edges plus memory buffer and backup selection
signatures.object: Recovery path and stopping behaviour of the agent
signatures.information: History; memory buffer of examined but rejected items.
signatures.operation: Permissible actions include going back to results or search; when the 13-transition mark is reached the agent is forced to choose from its buffer (backup strategy), up to 15 transitions in total.
signatures.output: Final item selection at stop or forced stop.
signatures.feedback: Observation after each action; no explicit error signal.
signatures.selection_rule_data: Heuristic forced choice from history when budget is exhausted.
signatures.failure_boundary: Number of backtracking events and recovery success are not reported.

signatures.name: State-specific zero-shot instruction instead of in-context examples
signatures.object: Source of task knowledge in the prompt
signatures.information: Author-written high-level rules per state (e.g. customisation options may cover a mismatch; do not reselect a clicked item).
signatures.operation: Replace one or more demonstration trajectories with per-state rules and layouts.
signatures.conditions: Rules are written by someone who knows the environment.
signatures.selection_rule_data: Hand-authored; dev-set use for prompt development not stated.
signatures.claimed_effect: Adding one in-context example does not help (50.0/74.9 vs 52.0/77.6 on 200 instructions).
signatures.failure_boundary: Difference within noise; human prior is still injected.

retention_trace.reason: Static prompt-design method; nothing is selected, persisted or reused across tasks, and the paper does not claim self-improvement.

gap.author_gap: Forward-only execution with oracle in-context trajectories cannot recover from mistakes or handle scenarios not covered by examples; a global action space lets the model take invalid actions.
gap.checked_gap: The authors observed invalid actions and stuck loops in their own ReAct rerun (anecdotal; no baseline invalid-action rate). The rerun scored below the originally reported ReAct, so the baseline may be weaker than the original in this setup. The two limitations are plausible but only the second is directly supported by the paper (valid actions 100% for LASER).

gap.residue: Hand annotated state set; a single domain; recovery behaviour unmeasured; costs unreported; WebArena-style multi-site tasks untested.
gap.stakes: Invalid or looping actions waste the step budget and lower success; on a real site some actions have irreversible effects.
gap.method_response: Per-state instructions and per-state function lists make invalid actions impossible by construction at the interface level and give explicit back transitions.
gap.remaining_gap: No demonstrated benefit of the state formulation over the same instructions in a flat prompt; no cost; no unseen domains; manual effort.
gap.current_relevance: SteP (2310.03720, same batch, later) lists LASER under defining state machines and contrasts its policy-stack control, so the control-structure line continued with dynamic call stacks; I did not open later pinned works for this paper.

claims.text: LASER outperforms prior methods on WebShop: 50.0 success / 75.6 reward vs ReAct 34.0/59.7 (rerun), ASH 30.2/56.7, WebGUM 45.0/67.5.
claims.setting: WebShop simulated shopping site, 500 test instructions, GPT-4-0613 with function calling, at most 15 transitions.
claims.baseline_control: ReAct rerun with GPT-4-0613 and added instructions; ReAct (PaLM, simplified), ASH, WebGUM numbers from prior papers; human expert 59.6/82.1.
claims.selection_vs_test: Test set 500 used for headline; prompt development split not stated; a Dev set is used for error analysis.
claims.result_denominator: n=500 per method; one run; SE about 2.2 points.
claims.counterevidence: ReAct rerun below the original ReAct (E010); LASER prompts carry rich domain rules and function calling (E014, E019); 5-point gap to WebGUM is about 1.6 SE (E034).
claims.allowed_conclusion: On WebShop, a GPT-4-0613 prompt design with hand-written state rules and function-call actions scores clearly above the authors own ReAct rerun and above reported ASH; superiority over the fine-tuned WebGUM is suggestive only. The state-space formulation as the cause is not isolated.

claims.text: On amazon.com LASER reaches 62.0 SR / 85.4 reward, close to the human 65.0 / 88.2.
claims.setting: First 100 WebShop test instructions run on amazon.com pages converted to the WebShop format, buying blocked, manual annotation by the authors.
claims.baseline_control: Human numbers from the WebShop paper.
claims.selection_vs_test: Site not used in building the system.
claims.counterevidence: Authors annotate their own outputs; no date; stronger search engine on Amazon (authors note); human reference not rerun.
claims.allowed_conclusion: On a small author-annotated sample, performance on amazon.com in the converted format is not distinguishable from the human figure.

claims.text: Zero-shot state instructions beat adding an in-context example; function calling and a stronger LLM help.
claims.counterevidence: Differences of 1.6-2.0 points at n=200 are within one SE; text-davinci-003 drop (38.5) is large.
claims.allowed_conclusion: Only the text-davinci-003 drop is clearly outside noise; one-shot and no-function-call effects are unresolved.

claims.text: The state formulation makes the agent always select valid actions and recover from mistakes by backtracking.
claims.baseline_control: Qualitative statements about ReAct invalid actions and loops.
claims.result_denominator: No count of invalid actions for any method and no count of backtracking events.
claims.counterevidence: Valid-action property comes from the function list, so it is true by construction; recovery is asserted not measured.
claims.allowed_conclusion: Valid actions are guaranteed by the interface; the recovery benefit is untested.

assessment.author_claim_preserved: state-space exploration formulation significantly outperforms previous methods and closes the gap with human performance on web navigation
assessment.strongest_supported_claim: In the WebShop simulator (500 test instructions) a GPT-4-0613 agent with hand-written state-specific instructions and per-state function-call actions scores 50.0% success / 75.6 reward, above the authors reproduced ReAct (34.0/59.7); on 100 author-annotated amazon.com instructions its 62.0% is indistinguishable from the reported human 65.0%. Whether the state-space formulation, backtracking, function calling, domain-specific rules or the backbone produces this is not established, and generalisation beyond shopping is untested.
unresolved: no same-prompt ablation of state graph / action restriction / backtracking
assessment.reproduction: No reproduction run; author reports only.

G.reason: Two concrete limitations (forward-only execution, global action space) with observed ReAct failures and a clearly named nearest neighbour (Synapse); lineage is acceptable, but the invalid-action prevalence of the baseline is not quantified and the baseline rerun is weaker than its original.

M.reason: The operation (state-specific prompt plus restricted action list with back transitions) addresses invalid actions directly and recovery plausibly, and the reasoning is easy to reconstruct. It does not yield a distinguishing measurable prediction about backtracking that is then tested.

X.reason: Prompts, state-action table, backup strategy, step budget and model are fully disclosed, which is unusually reconstructable; missing items are sampling temperature, the exact fourth state, and boundary conditions beyond the Limitations paragraph.

E.measurement.reason: WebShop reward and success are programmatic with ground-truth targets in the simulator, but the authors report that 9/30 sampled errors were arguably correct items, the live-site evaluation is self-annotated by the authors, and the main baseline rerun underperforms its original.

E.causality.reason: No ablation removes the state formulation, per-state action restriction or backtracking while keeping the same instructions; the controlled variables that are ablated (one-shot, function calling) are inside noise; the main comparison also changes the backbone and added domain rules.

E.holdout.reason: Test set evaluated once and a different site (amazon.com) was not used to build the system, which counts as real out-of-environment evidence; but the transfer is 100 self-annotated instructions in the same converted format, the prompt-development split is not stated, and only one domain is covered.

E.statistics.reason: Single runs, n=100/200 with differences smaller than one SE interpreted as findings, no seeds or variance, failure audit of 30 dev errors with category counts.

E.cost.reason: No token, latency, dollar or LLM-call counts for LASER or baselines are reported although the method uses GPT-4 with several prompts and function calls per step and the intro motivates fewer examples by cost.

status_reason: Complete paper including all appendices and prompts read; three figures unavailable as text. All eight items resolved; cost recorded as not_reported after the scope above was searched.
readable_summary: System method (state-conditioned prompting), score 58.8 (58.75), online WebShop, claim scoped. Prompts fully disclosed and WebShop scoring is programmatic; but no ablation removes the state graph / action restriction / backtracking, the ReAct rerun is weaker than its original, ablation gaps are within noise, amazon.com is a 100-instruction author-annotated sample, and cost is not reported.
